description: The life of a nonce inside the gateway: what it became, what it cost, and what settlement will credit for it. Every panel explains itself under its info icon.

panels.description: The epoch the gateway believes the chain is in. Escrow rotation happens around epoch transitions, so a burst of burns beside a change here is expected rather than alarming.
panels.title: Epoch

panels.description: 1 while the chain is refusing inference work, which happens during proof-of-compute. Not a fault — but nothing is served until it clears.
panels.title: Requests blocked

panels.description: How old the gateway's picture of the chain is. Capacity, epoch phase and blocking are all decided from it, so a growing age means those decisions rest on stale state.
panels.title: Snapshot age

panels.description: The chain's own high-water mark for nonces. The ledger derives assigned counts from it, so a flat line while traffic flows means the gateway's chain reads have stalled.
panels.title: Highest nonce the chain has seen
2 · The fleet: what is serving right now

panels.description: How many escrows will take a request right now. An escrow leaves this count the moment it stops accepting, which happens before it is retired — so a drop here is the earliest sign one is going away.
panels.title: Escrows accepting

panels.description: Not requests in flight. A nonce is counted until its chain vote is posted, which is long after the client has its answer.
panels.title: Nonces the chain is still owed

panels.description: Escrows where at least one participant is unavailable. The executor of a nonce is fixed by nonce mod group_size, so a blocked participant does not shift load elsewhere: the nonces falling to that slot cannot be served at all.
panels.title: Escrows with a blocked participant

panels.description: One row per escrow. accepting says whether it will take a new request right now — an escrow stops accepting before it is retired, so 'draining' here is the earliest sign one is going away. weight is what the picker multiplies by: a zero-weight escrow is skipped by every pick while looking healthy everywhere else.
panels.title: Escrow by escrow

panels.description: The effective host weight behind each escrow. Zero means every pick skips it — usually because its participant membership never reached the capacity layer, which is silent everywhere else.
panels.title: Escrow weight the picker sees

panels.description: Not requests. Spread of unsettled nonces across escrows; one escrow carrying everything usually means the others have lost weight or membership.
panels.title: Nonces still owed, per escrow

panels.description: Slots whose participant is unavailable. Each one is a fraction of the escrow's nonces that cannot be served, because a nonce chooses its executor arithmetically.
panels.title: Blocked participants per escrow

panels.description: The escrow hold a race takes is released only once the timeout vote for every unfinished nonce has been posted, and the gateway sleeps until the chain's deadline before it may post one: the refusal window for a nonce that never got a receipt, the execution window for one that did. So these lines keep counting long after the clients were answered — a request served in seconds can hold a nonce for minutes.
panels.title: Nonces still owed against the votes they wait on

panels.description: Nonces one client request costs: attempts that reached a host plus nonces burned without sending anything. Both spend a nonce, so both belong here. 1.0 is one nonce per request; above that is speculation, retries and burns, and the speculative share lands in the finished_unused bucket below. Below 1.0 is possible only if requests are being answered from the cache, which costs no nonce at all.
panels.title: Nonces per request

panels.description: Nonces spent per request without sending any work — throttling, an unavailable host, a capability mismatch. They produce no answer for anyone and settlement pays for them anyway.
panels.title: Burns per request

panels.description: Why each attempt was sent to a host. Only attempts that actually reached the network are counted, so this is the numerator of nonces-per-request minus the burns. A speculative reason is a second nonce spent to protect one answer.
panels.title: Attempts sent, by why

panels.description: Terminal state of every attempt: won, lost, or a failure kind. Lost attempts did real work the client never received.
panels.title: Attempts by how they ended

panels.description: How long the host took to acknowledge the nonce at all. This is the deadline the escalation ladder reads first: when it runs past its budget the gateway starts a second attempt, spending another nonce. High receipt with normal first-content means the host is queueing, not generating. The mean is drawn beside the quantiles on purpose: a quantile cannot report above the histogram's highest bucket, so it pins flat when attempts run longer than the buckets reach, while the mean keeps rising. The two separating is the signal that the buckets are too short. These are distributions, not cases: they say how the fleet behaves, not which request was slow. The log panel below this section is where a single request, its tokens, its escrow and its outcome live.
panels.title: Receipt · p50 and p95

panels.description: Time until the first token of the answer appeared. Measures the host's prefill, which scales with the prompt rather than with the answer. The mean is drawn beside the quantiles on purpose: a quantile cannot report above the histogram's highest bucket, so it pins flat when attempts run longer than the buckets reach, while the mean keeps rising. The two separating is the signal that the buckets are too short. These are distributions, not cases: they say how the fleet behaves, not which request was slow. The log panel below this section is where a single request, its tokens, its escrow and its outcome live.
panels.title: First content · p50 and p95

panels.description: End to end duration of one attempt per participant. The slowest line here is the participant the race keeps having to work around. The mean is drawn beside the quantiles on purpose: a quantile cannot report above the histogram's highest bucket, so it pins flat when attempts run longer than the buckets reach, while the mean keeps rising. The two separating is the signal that the buckets are too short. These are distributions, not cases: they say how the fleet behaves, not which request was slow. The log panel below this section is where a single request, its tokens, its escrow and its outcome live.
panels.title: Whole attempt · p95 per participant

panels.description: Why the gateway burned a nonce instead of sending work: no PoC-eligible host, participant throttled, participant ejected, capability mismatch, no compatible request after a stale hold, or a caller that vanished before dispatch.
panels.title: Nonces burned without work, by reason

panels.description: The same burns as the panel above, split by the participant whose slot the nonce landed on. A validator holding several slots of the group costs one nonce per slot every time a request refuses it, so a single host can dominate this without being a majority of the fleet.
panels.title: Nonces burned without work, by host
6 · Timeouts: the only thing that undoes a charge

panels.description: started is an attempt to vote, completed means the vote reached the chain and a miss was recorded, failed and skipped mean it did not — and that nonce settles as work the participant never did. The gap between started and completed is money.
panels.title: Timeout funnel

panels.description: insufficient votes is the one to watch: it is structural, not transient. If the escrow's verifiers cannot reach the threshold, no retry ever fixes it and every unfinished nonce on that escrow is paid for. The escrow and nonce are in the log line timeout_insufficient_votes.
panels.title: Why a timeout did not apply
7 · Errors and what the client saw

panels.description: Why individual attempts failed. Most are invisible to the client because another attempt answered — but each one spent a nonce.
panels.title: Attempt failures by reason

panels.description: HTTP status the participant returned, which separates a host that refused from a host that was unreachable. A wall of one status against one participant is that host, not the network.
panels.title: Transport errors by status

panels.description: The executor's own stamp on the receipt it signs before inference, against the midpoint of the round trip that carried it. The stamp is whole seconds and truncates downward, so half a second is added back — without it every correctly-set clock reads a second slow. What remains is real drift, and host_receipt_ms is how sharply it can be read: the wider the round trip, the softer the number. Needs a gateway build that logs host_clock_offset_ms.
panels.title: Host clock drift, against the receipt window

panels.description: Requests answered normally while an attempt inside them failed. Nobody complains about these, and they are the earliest visible sign of a sick participant — paid for in nonces the whole time.
panels.title: Failures the client never saw

panels.description: Requests that ended with nothing useful for the caller, beside the overall request outcome mix for scale.
panels.title: Failures the client did see
8 · Pressure: what the gateway is refusing

panels.description: The budget gate. When in-flight reaches the ceiling, arrivals queue rather than fail, and the queue is the first line. A queue that never drains means the ceiling is below what callers are sending.
panels.title: Queue depth against the admission ceiling

panels.description: A held nonce is bound to a host and waiting for a compatible request rather than being burned. An exhausted burn budget means the escrow stopped spending nonces on requests it cannot serve — occasional is healthy, constant means that escrow's hosts are gone.
panels.title: Nonces held and budgets exhausted

panels.description: The host gate. The window is how many requests a participant may hold at once and grows while it succeeds; the breaker opens after repeated failures and shuts that participant out for a backoff. In-flight pinned to window means this participant is the bottleneck.
panels.title: Participant breakers

panels.description: ejected: hosts the outlier detector pulled out of rotation for answering far slower than their peers. exhausted: hosts whose concurrency window is full, so nothing more can be sent to them right now. tracked: how many hosts exist to send to at all. Watch the gap: when ejected plus exhausted approaches tracked, the shard is running out of places to put work, and requests start queueing behind hosts rather than being spread across them.
panels.title: Hosts the gateway has stopped using

panels.description: A steady host and one that sends a chunk then stops carry the same chunk count; the silence between chunks is what parts them. The solid line is the longest silence inside one attempt, the dashed one the average gap — the inverse of the delivered rate. The silence before [DONE] is not counted.
panels.title: How long a host goes quiet mid-answer

panels.description: The client's own wall clock, from dispatch to the last byte it received. This is the number a user would quote, and it is not what the in-flight panels show: those keep counting the nonce until its chain vote lands. Needs a gateway build that logs duration_ms.
panels.title: How long the client actually waited

panels.description: Every escalation spends another nonce. A single reason dominating means the race is hedging on one deadline, not on host trouble.
panels.title: Escalations by what triggered them

panels.description: The share of escalations blamed on the first-token wait. Well above half means engine_first_token_floor_ms is shorter than the fleet's real time to first token.
panels.title: Hedges the first-token deadline caused

panels.description: Attempts started divided by requests answered successfully. This is what engine_max_attempts_per_request bounds; near that bound means most requests use their whole budget.
panels.title: Attempts spent per answer delivered
10 · What the limiter refuses, and the cap behind it

panels.description: The gateway limiter's own refusals, before any host is chosen. concurrent_requests and queue_depth are different problems: the first is capacity, the second is patience.
panels.title: Requests turned away, by which cap

panels.description: The concurrency ceiling a model is judged against, drawn beside its actual load. Refusals while the two lines are far apart mean the cap shrank, not that traffic grew.
panels.title: The cap in force against what is in flight

panels.description: Total weight counts only hosts the participant limiter calls available, baseline counts them all. A gap between the two is the gateway shrinking its own ceiling because breakers are open.
panels.title: Host weight the cap is derived from

panels.description: 1 while the chain has reported no weights for a model, so escrow scoring runs on membership share instead. Every capacity number above is a guess while this is up.
panels.title: Models scoring on the membership fallback

panels.description: Healthy drops to 0 when a refresh fails; the gateway then serves the last known phase until the staleness gate refuses admission. The block reason says which gate is closed.
panels.title: Chain snapshot: fresh, and what is blocking

panels.description: Live total against GATEWAY_MAX_BUFFERED_RESPONSE_BYTES. Approaching the budget refuses new non-streaming replies rather than growing memory.
panels.title: Bytes held for replies being assembled

panels.description: An SSE event too large for the per-attempt carry budget. Anything sustained here means classification is dropping events, so content and usage detection are unreliable for that host.
panels.title: Reassembly buffers that overflowed their budget

panels.description: The request records' write rate and their losses by cause. A non-zero loss line means some served requests have no record behind GET /v1/requests/{id}.
panels.title: Ledger rows written against rows lost
12 · What the host signed, what the cache kept, and how hosts are reached

panels.description: Every completed stream the session compared with the Finish its host signed. Any mismatch means a host served bytes it did not sign for; each one costs that host an unresponsive sample.
panels.title: Served streams checked against their Finish

panels.description: Stored, or the reason it refused. A rising unfinished_answer means hosts end streams without a finish_reason.
panels.title: What the response cache did with each reply

panels.description: New escrow-host pairs per second, by whether the host was reached over Connect on HTTP/2 (h2) or fell back to JSON. JSON on a v6 fleet means a host is not publishing its peer RPC.
panels.title: Escrow-to-host bindings by path

panels.description: Hosts a live escrow binds, counted by mode. Series disappear when the last escrow binding a host retires.
panels.title: Hosts by how live escrows reach them

title: Gonka gateway — escrows
